TODAY, when money moved in or out in amounts large enough that WHEN it moved would decide the percentage, the Return states nothing and the screen shows the dollar walk alone. That person — someone actively adding money — is the one who most needs a rate and currently never sees one.
HIS RULING: show the exact rate there instead. Where the walk now says there is no percentage, it will read that counting when you added money, the rate was X% a year.
WHY THIS IS SAFE, measured: the two methods are not different answers. The window Return divides the gain once by a straight-line average of the money at work; the money-weighted rate compounds each amount over its own days and solves for the rate. On $100,000 with $10,000 added on 1 July and $118,000 at the end, they give 7.6161% and 7.6341% — 0.018 of a percentage point apart. They can never be far apart, because the window Return REFUSES the moment its straight-line shortcut could be off by more than a percentage point. So this fills the gap it leaves and never contradicts it: one return is visible at a time.
WHERE IT CAME FROM: the figure was built 2026-07-14 as its own card on the old Invest screen, and the Performance design he approved on 2026-09-25 (mock v14) removed that card. The function has been correct and reached by no screen since.

rows.subject: In the time-weighted return, money that moves on a day counts for that whole day
rows.plain: The time-weighted return counts money that arrives on a day as there for that whole day, and money taken out as gone for that whole day: that day's growth is the evening value ÷ (the previous evening's value + money added − money taken out) − 1. A new account opened with $10,000 and worth $10,050 that evening returned +0.50% that day (+$50); worth $9,800, −2.00% (−$200). Vanguard worth $50,000, $10,000 added in the morning, $60,300 that evening: +0.50% (the $300 was earned on $60,000). Before: the money counted as arriving at the end of the day — the first deposit into a new account could not be measured at all, a value below the money just added was refused as a broken record, and the Vanguard day read +0.60%.

rows.subject: A bond's or CD's return counts the interest it paid; its line shows face, coupon and YTM; the account page's window bar shows the app's own figures
rows.plain: Three parts. (a) A bond's or CD's return over a window is its price change PLUS the interest it was paid in the window: interest and coupon records dated on or after the window's first day that name that holding (or, naming no holding, sit in an account that is that one bond or CD). Return = (1 + price change) × (1 + interest ÷ value today) − 1, which is (value today + interest) ÷ value at the start − 1. KeyBank CD $5,000, price flat, $100 interest → +2.00%; US Treasury $4,000, $85 → +2.125%, shown +2.13%; the Bonds & CDs bar $9,000, $185 → +2.06%. Only an individual bond or CD counts its interest this way (Bonds & CDs, no fund word in its name, not a Treasury-bill ETF, and a CD type, a 9-character security id, a maturity date, a coupon rate or a face value to say it is one instrument); a bond fund's distributions are already in its adjusted closes (DEC-4644), so nothing is counted twice. An account's own time-weighted return (DEC-4439) measures its whole value, the interest that landed in its cash included, and does not change. (b) The columns keep one meaning each (DEC-0093): MARKET VALUE is market value and adds up to the account; RETURN is the window return with interest. The line under a bond's or CD's name shows its face value, coupon rate and yield to maturity, as a stock's shows its shares: $5,000 face · 4.00% · YTM 4.00%. A bank CD's yield to maturity is its rate; a part not given is left out. (c) The account-page drawing's window bar on every state (A to E) is the app's own figure, read off the built screen with each state's data; a window the app greys is a dash, and the grey placeholders are gone.

rows.subject: A window that opens before the daily record begins is joined at the record's first day: the days before it are worked back from price history, then the record's own return
rows.plain: Where a window's first day is before the daily record begins, its return is two parts multiplied: the days before the record's first day, worked back from each holding's price history (holdings with a history only, DEC-5068 and DEC-5291; a bond's or CD's interest added, DEC-6212), and the record's own time-weighted return from its first day to today (DEC-4439), the one Since shows. Return = (1 + the days before) × (1 + the record's part) − 1. The walk is joined the same way: its beginning is the record's first value worked back over the days before it (less what the holdings gained then and the money moved then), then the record's walk; it still adds up to today's ending. Only holdings held on the record's first day count in the days before it (one bought later had no part in them); an account the record holds later counts only if the record's part works it back on its own. The left-out sentence is DEC-6076's, said of the days before the record only, and only when those days are worked back: "Before Oct 1, 2025, when the daily record begins: Return is on the $X with a price history. <name> ($Y) has no price history, so its gains are not included." Its amounts are today's values, as DEC-6076 has them: $X = today's value of the holdings the days before count; $Y = today's value of each one left out. Example, the account-page drawing's state A: the record begins Oct 1, 2025; 1Y's beginning is Sep 29, 2025; VOO's price history holds $522.43 on Sep 29 and no close again until Dec 31, so VOO moved 0.00% over those days; the bonds were bought Apr 2, 2026, so they had no part. 1Y = (1 + 0.00%) × (1 + 8.26%) − 1 = +8.26%, the same as Since (was +7.12%); 2Y = (522.43 ÷ 460.00) × 1.0826 − 1 = +22.95%, a year over 731 days +10.87% (was +9.57%). Unchanged: a record that begins today (DEC-5291's answer — state D's 1Y +10.00%), a record that reaches back the whole window (the measured return), and a window whose days before the record cannot be worked back (nothing with a history there: DEC-5291's answer, or its refusal).
